title: Given a binary tree and an array of numbers representing a sequence, determine whether there exists a root-to-leaf path such that the node values along the path exactly match the sequence in order and length. Explain how an index into the sequence tracks progress during the depth-first search.
shortTitle: Path With Given Sequence (Does a Root-to-Leaf Path Match an Exact Sequence?)

s1_definition.profdef: Path With Given Sequence is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we match node values against a fixed target sequence while descending. We carry an index into the sequence. At each node we check that the node's value equals the sequence element at the current index; if it does not, that branch fails immediately. The path succeeds only at a leaf where the index has consumed exactly the whole sequence. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a payment must travel through an exact pre-approved sequence of desk codes, like a mandated handshake. We are given the required sequence and the desk tree, and we check whether any full top-to-bottom chain matches the sequence step for step, no more and no less. We walk down comparing each desk code to the next expected code, and if we ever mismatch we abandon that chain.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match node values against the sequence by index as you descend, and succeed only when a leaf lands exactly at the end of the sequence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Path With Given Sequence is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we match node values against a fixed target sequence while descending. We carry an index into the sequence. At each node we check that the node's value equals the sequence element at the current index; if it does not, that branch fails immediately. The path succeeds only at a leaf where the index has consumed exactly the whole sequence. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a payment must travel through an exact pre-approved sequence of desk codes, like a mandated handshake. We are given the required sequence and the desk tree, and we check whether any full top-to-bottom chain matches the sequence step for step, no more and no less. We walk down comparing each desk code to the next expected code, and if we ever mismatch we abandon that chain.

**One line to remember:** Match node values against the sequence by index as you descend, and succeed only when a leaf lands exactly at the end of the sequence.

sections.s2_technical:
We pass an integer `index` that tracks how far into the sequence we have matched. The first guard rejects impossible states: if the node is null, or the index has run past the sequence length, or the node's value does not equal `sequence[index]`, we return false. For example, `if (node == null || index >= seq.length || node.value != seq[index]) return false;` combines all three failure cases cleanly.

The success test happens at a leaf, where we must have matched the final element and have no sequence left over. For example, `if (node.isLeaf() && index == seq.length - 1) return true;`. For internal nodes we recurse into both children with `index + 1` and OR the results, because any single matching path is enough.

A senior-level nuance is the exact-length requirement. A path that matches the sequence as a prefix but continues past it is not a match, and a path that ends before consuming the sequence is not a match either. Both are handled: a too-long path fails the `index >= seq.length` guard at the extra node, and a too-short path fails because the leaf test requires `index == seq.length - 1`. Another nuance is short-circuit evaluation, so the first matching path stops the search.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A high-value payment from Rajesh at the National Bank of India must follow an exact mandated routing of desk codes for regulatory compliance, for instance the sequence must be head office, then regional, then a specific signing desk. Operations has the desk tree and the mandated sequence and must confirm that at least one real chain follows the sequence precisely. This is exactly how Path With Given Sequence works: the mandated codes are the sequence, and a matching leaf chain proves compliance.

Problem 2 — A chain that matches the first few codes but then continues to an extra desk is a violation, not a pass. This is why the leaf test demands that the sequence be fully and exactly consumed, rejecting both too-long and too-short chains.

The code defines a `DeskNode` with an integer desk code. A `SequencePathService` exposes `hasMandatedPath(root, sequence)` returning a boolean. A `Demo` builds a tree and checks one matching sequence and one that is a prefix only, proving the prefix is rejected.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: tree root 10, left 20 with leaf 40, right 30; sequence {10, 20, 40}.

Step 1: Enter root 10 at index 0. seq[0] is 10, matches. Not a leaf, recurse left into 20 with index 1 and right into 30 with index 1.

Step 2: Enter 20 at index 1. seq[1] is 20, matches. Not a leaf, recurse left into 40 with index 2.

Step 3: Enter 40 at index 2. seq[2] is 40, matches. 40 is a leaf and index 2 equals seq.length minus one, so return true.

Step 4: The true result short-circuits, so the right subtree 30 is never explored. Final answer true.

For the second sequence {10, 20}: root matches at index 0, node 20 matches at index 1, but 20 is not a leaf, so the leaf test never fires; descending to 40 at index 2 overruns the sequence and fails, so the overall answer is false.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Path With Given Sequence asks whether any root-to-leaf path in a binary tree matches a fixed target sequence exactly, both in order and in length. I solve it with a depth-first traversal that carries an index into the sequence. At each node I reject immediately if the node is null, if the index has run past the sequence, or if the node's value differs from the sequence element at the current index. I declare success only at a leaf where the index sits on the last element, and for internal nodes I recurse into both children with the index advanced by one and combine with a logical OR so a single matching chain is enough.

The subtlety I always highlight is that the match must be exact. A path that matches the sequence as a prefix but then continues to an extra node is not a match, and a path that ends before the sequence is consumed is not a match either. My guards handle both: an overrunning path trips the index-past-length check, and a short path never satisfies the leaf test that requires the index to equal the last position.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enforce mandated routing for high-value payments, where a payment from Rajesh had to travel through an exact regulator-approved sequence of desk codes. I modelled each desk as a node with an integer code, drove the depth-first search with an index into the mandated sequence, and returned true only when a real chain consumed the sequence exactly at a leaf. Explaining the exact-length rule and the index-driven matching, including why a prefix match is a compliance failure, is what demonstrates to an interviewer that I understand both the algorithm and the regulatory consequence of getting it wrong.
